name: Cod liver oil

lead: Cod liver oil is a fish-liver supplement supplying omega-3 fats plus vitamins A and D. It has a long history as a folk and bottled remedy and helped lead to the discovery of vitamins A and D.
No trial was found testing it for appearance outcomes. Human studies have looked at blood lipids, platelet function and childhood outcomes instead.

paras: EPA and DHA are incorporated into blood and cell lipids with supplementation, as one human study reported. Vitamin D supports bone mineralisation, and its use against rickets is the best-documented historical effect.

Vitamin A accumulates in the liver, and Wikipedia reports a tablespoon exceeds the adult tolerable upper limit and children's limits several-fold. Excess preformed vitamin A can cause nausea, skin peeling, bone pain and liver damage.

lead: Cod liver oil is a dietary supplement made from the liver of Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua). Like other fish oils it contains the omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA, and unlike most it also contains substantial vitamins A and D.[1][2] One tablespoon (13.6 g) provides about 4,080 micrograms of vitamin A and 34 micrograms (1,360 IU) of vitamin D according to USDA figures cited by Wikipedia.[1]

It was used in northern European folk medicine for rheumatism and became a bottled remedy in the nineteenth century, and it played a part in the discovery of vitamins A and D.[1] In looksmaxxing and diet communities it is discussed as a vitamin A and D source, often alongside Weston A. Price-style diets.

Trials from the 1980s examined its effects on blood lipids and platelet function, and observational work examined childhood outcomes.[3][4][5] The sources reviewed contain no trial testing it for appearance. One tablespoon exceeds the adult tolerable upper intake for vitamin A, which is why vitamin A toxicity is the principal safety concern.[1][6]
infobox: EPA, DHA, vitamin A, vitamin D

paras: Cod liver oil is roughly 20% omega-3 by composition and has higher vitamin A and D levels than other fish oils with similar fatty-acid profiles.[1] Because the vitamin content varies by product, labels differ.

Northern European communities applied the oil to skin and took it orally for rheumatism and gout.[1] From the 1820s researchers in Germany noted that children given the oil did not develop rickets, and it became a 19th-century patent medicine and bottled remedy.[1] In 1899 London surgeon John Bland-Sutton used it for rickets in lion cubs at the London Zoo.[1] Norwegian pharmacist Peter Moller devised a steam extraction process in 1850 that made the oil more palatable.[1][2]

In 1914 Elmer McCollum and Marguerite Davis identified what became vitamin A, and in 1922 McCollum showed the rickets-curing factor was a distinct vitamin he named D.[1] After the Second World War, synthetic vitamin supplements reduced its popularity.[2]

Wikipedia reports cod liver oil may be beneficial as secondary prevention after a heart attack, benefits for psoriasis in a 2005 study, and an association with lower rates of severe depression in the 2007 Hordaland Health Study.[1] A topical product containing petrolatum and cod liver oil is labelled in the US to protect minor cuts, scrapes, burns and chapped skin.[7]

Grokipedia notes mixed evidence for cardiovascular benefit and that some recent studies suggest possible increased atrial fibrillation or stroke risk in healthy populations; this is an AI-generated source and the claim is not independently verified here.[2]

Vitamin A accumulates in the liver and excess preformed vitamin A causes hypervitaminosis A.[1] One tablespoon contains 136% of the adult tolerable upper limit, 680% of the limit for ages 1 to 3 and 453% for ages 4 to 8, and a teaspoon daily exceeds the limit for children aged 1 to 8.[1] Hypervitaminosis A symptoms include nausea, headache, skin peeling, bone pain and liver damage.[1]

No studies found testing cod liver oil for appearance outcomes such as skin, hair or facial features. Human studies of the oil for other outcomes include a 1985 study in six volunteers supplemented for five months, which found incorporation of EPA and DHA into blood lipids and lowered triglycerides,[3] and a 1981 study in healthy young men on blood lipids and haemostasis.[4] A population-based case-control study reported that cod liver oil use in the first year of life was associated with lower risk of childhood-onset type 1 diabetes.[5] A 1986 New England Journal of Medicine study reported inhibition of atherosclerosis in a swine model, which is animal research.[8]

Registered trials include a large phase 4 study of cod liver oil for COVID-19 prevention (NCT04609423, n=47,210),[9] a bioavailability study of vitamin D in cod liver oil and multivitamin tablets in Norway (NCT01482689),[10] and a trial in periodontitis using omega-3 fatty acids.[11] Registry entries in the sources reviewed do not report results.
